title: Representations and contextual expressions

worked_examples.q: A library charges R4 per printed page. Write the cost for n pages.

steps.title: Count equal groups
steps.action: Place one four-rand tile under each page.
steps.narration: The number of pages tells us how many copies of four rand to use.

steps.title: Name the cost
steps.action: Multiply four by n.
steps.narration: The answer is a cost in rand, not a page count.

worked_examples.verify: For n=3, three pages cost R12; 4(3)=12.
worked_examples.misconception: Writing 4+n instead of four per page.
worked_examples.repair: Draw one price tile for every page.

worked_examples.q: A delivery costs R10 plus R3 per kilometre. Write the cost for k kilometres.
states: Fixed R10; R3 for each of k km

steps.title: Build the distance part
steps.action: Give every kilometre its three-rand tile.
steps.narration: Three times k varies with distance.

steps.title: Attach the one fixed charge
steps.action: Add ten rand once to the variable total.
steps.narration: The starting fee does not repeat for every kilometre.

worked_examples.misconception: Multiplying the fixed R10 by k.
worked_examples.repair: Place the fixed tile outside the repeated kilometres.

worked_examples.q: A flow machine doubles x, then adds 5. Write its output rule and find the output for x=3.

steps.title: Follow the first arrow
steps.action: Doubling x gives two x.
steps.narration: The first action is multiplication.

steps.title: Follow the second arrow
steps.action: Add five after doubling.
steps.narration: Operation order matters; add five only at the end.

steps.title: Try a concrete input
steps.action: Three doubles to six, then plus five is eleven.
steps.narration: The rule and diagram agree for this input.

worked_examples.repair: Trace the arrows in their stated order.

worked_examples.skill: Infer a rule from a table
worked_examples.q: A table pairs x=1,2,3 with y=5,8,11. Write a linear rule and test x=4.

model.description: Infer a rule from a table

steps.title: Compare successive rows
steps.action: Each next output rises by three when x rises by one.
steps.narration: The variable contribution is three per input unit.

steps.title: Find the fixed offset
steps.action: At x one, three plus two makes five.
steps.narration: The offset is two, not five.

steps.title: Write the complete rule
steps.action: Combine three x with the two-unit start.
steps.narration: Check all three given rows.

steps.title: Extend one row
steps.action: At four the output is twelve plus two.
steps.narration: The new row tests the proposed rule.

worked_examples.misconception: Taking 5 as the starting amount at x=0.
worked_examples.repair: Run the three-times part backward to zero.

worked_examples.q: Tickets cost R6 each plus one booking fee of R4. Write C(t), then fill costs for t=1,2,3.
states: t tickets; R6 each plus R4 once

steps.title: Model each ticket
steps.action: Six times t gives the changing ticket total.
steps.narration: The number of tickets controls only this part.

steps.title: Attach the booking fee
steps.action: Add four once after ticket cost.
steps.narration: It is charged for the whole booking.

steps.title: Fill first two table rows
steps.action: At one ticket pay ten; at two pay sixteen.
steps.narration: Each additional ticket raises the bill by six.

steps.title: Fill the third row
steps.action: Eighteen plus four is twenty two.
steps.narration: Check the six-rand increase continues.

worked_examples.verify: For t=3, three R6 tickets cost R18 plus R4 fee = R22.
worked_examples.repair: Keep the fee tile separate from ticket columns.

worked_examples.q: A tank starts with 30 L and loses 2 L each minute. Write V(m) and find V(5). State a sensible domain.
states: Total loss after m minutes is 2m L

steps.title: Accumulate the loss
steps.action: Two litres leave in each minute, for m minutes.
steps.narration: The loss is two m litres.

steps.title: Subtract loss from the start
steps.action: Thirty minus two m is the remaining volume.
steps.narration: A loss lowers the total.

steps.title: Substitute five minutes
steps.action: Thirty minus ten leaves twenty litres.
steps.narration: Units remain litres.

steps.title: Bound the time
steps.action: After fifteen minutes the model reaches zero.
steps.narration: Negative time or negative physical volume is outside this scenario.

worked_examples.verify: Five losses of 2 L give 30−10=20 L; 15 losses give 0 L.
worked_examples.misconception: Adding a loss or accepting a negative tank volume.
worked_examples.repair: Animate each two-litre loss from the starting bar.

worked_examples.skill: Model repeated groups with an extra
worked_examples.q: A school buys p packs of 6 pencils and 4 loose pencils. Write the total and find it for p=3.

model.description: Model repeated groups with an extra

states: p groups of 6 and four loose

steps.title: Count pack pencils
steps.action: Each of p packs contains six pencils.
steps.narration: Multiply six by the pack count.

steps.title: Add loose pencils once
steps.action: The four loose pencils are outside the packs.
steps.narration: They are not four in each pack.

steps.title: Try three packs
steps.action: Eighteen packed plus four loose is twenty two.
steps.narration: Count the diagram independently.

worked_examples.misconception: Multiplying the four loose pencils by p.
worked_examples.repair: Keep loose pencils visually outside the pack boundaries.

worked_examples.q: A rectangle has length (x+3) cm and width x cm. Write a simplified perimeter rule and find P at x=4.
states: Rectangle sides x+3, x, x+3, x

steps.title: Trace each side
steps.action: Two sides are x plus three and two sides are x.
steps.narration: Perimeter follows the whole boundary.

steps.title: Collect like terms
steps.action: Four x pieces and two threes give four x plus six.
steps.narration: Do not leave out the opposite side.

steps.title: Measure at four
steps.action: Two sevens and two fours total twenty two centimetres.
steps.narration: Check the simplified rule gives the same length.

worked_examples.verify: At x=4 sides are 7,4,7,4 cm; total 22 cm; 4(4)+6=22.
worked_examples.misconception: Using area or only two sides.
worked_examples.repair: Trace four edges with distinct markers.

worked_examples.q: Plan A costs R20 plus R5 per visit; Plan B costs R8 per visit. Write both rules and compare for 4 visits.
worked_examples.answer: A(v)=20+5v, B(v)=8v; at v=4, A=R40 and B=R32, so B costs R8 less.
states: At v=4: B=32; B costs R8 less

steps.title: Build each plan separately
steps.action: A has a start fee plus visit fees; B has only visit fees.
steps.narration: Do not mix charges from different plans.

steps.title: Calculate A for four
steps.action: Four visits add twenty rand to the twenty-rand fee.
steps.narration: Plan A is forty rand.

steps.title: Calculate B and compare
steps.action: Four times eight is thirty two; the difference is eight rand.
steps.narration: This comparison is for four visits only.

worked_examples.misconception: Claiming one plan is always cheaper from one input.
worked_examples.repair: Keep parallel plan lanes and label the input.

worked_examples.q: A taxi charges R12 once and R4 per kilometre. A learner writes T(d)=16d. Find the first mistake and write the correct rule.
worked_examples.answer: The learner repeated the R12 fixed fee; T(d)=12+4d.
states: R12 is one fixed tile, not d tiles

steps.title: Inspect the learner rule
steps.action: Sixteen d multiplies both fee and distance by d.
steps.narration: The R12 start charge does not repeat.

steps.title: Rebuild the changing part
steps.action: Only four rand per kilometre becomes four d.
steps.narration: Distance controls the variable part.

steps.title: Place the one-off fee
steps.action: Attach twelve once to four d.
steps.narration: The corrected expression is twelve plus four d.

worked_examples.verify: At d=2, taxi costs R12+R8=R20; claim 16(2)=R32.
worked_examples.misconception: Combining fixed and per-unit prices before multiplying.
worked_examples.repair: Move the fixed tile outside the distance row.

worked_examples.skill: Compare equivalent verbal and formula rules
worked_examples.q: A savings rule says “start with R7 and add R5 each week”. Another says S(w)=5(w+1)+2. Are the rules equivalent for every w?

model.description: Compare equivalent verbal and formula rules

steps.title: Build the verbal path
steps.action: The start is seven and each week adds five.
steps.narration: Seven is a fixed amount.

steps.title: Expand the formula path
steps.action: Five multiplies w and one, then two remains.
steps.narration: Five multiplies both w and one, so the formula becomes five w plus five plus two.

steps.title: Compare general expressions
steps.action: Five w plus seven appears in both paths.
steps.narration: The rules agree for every permitted week count.

worked_examples.verify: At w=2 both give R17; distribution proves equality for every w.
worked_examples.misconception: Treating one matching week as proof for all weeks.
worked_examples.repair: Show the symbolic expansion before a numerical check.

worked_examples.skill: Translate a table with a missing input
worked_examples.q: A shop charges R9 once plus R3 per item. Complete the total for 2, 4 and n items, then find the total for n=7.
worked_examples.answer: 2 items R15; 4 items R21; n items R(9+3n); 7 items R30.

model.description: Translate a table with a missing input

steps.title: Make the general rule
steps.action: The one-off nine stays outside the three-per-item term.
steps.narration: A letter can stand for any item count.

steps.title: Fill two concrete rows
steps.action: Two items add six, four items add twelve.
steps.narration: Each row applies the same rule.

steps.title: Test seven items
steps.action: Nine plus twenty one equals thirty.
steps.narration: Check the three-rand steps from the table.

worked_examples.misconception: Mistaking the R9 for a per-item price.

worked_examples.q: A rectangular garden has length (x+2) m and width 3 m. Write and simplify its area; find area when x=4.

steps.title: Split the length
steps.action: Partition the rectangle into x metres and two metres.
steps.narration: Both regions share the three-metre width.

steps.title: Calculate both regions
steps.action: Areas are three x and six square metres.
steps.narration: Area units are square metres, not metres.

steps.title: Test at four
steps.action: Length is six metres, so three times six is eighteen square metres.
steps.narration: The split regions give twelve plus six.

worked_examples.verify: At x=4, full rectangle 6×3=18 m²; split 12+6=18 m².

worked_examples.skill: Distinguish two flows with the same inputs
worked_examples.q: Machine A adds 4 then doubles; Machine B doubles then adds 4. Write both rules and compare outputs at x=5.

model.description: Distinguish two flows with the same inputs

steps.title: Trace each arrow order
steps.action: A doubles the whole x plus four; B adds four after doubling.
steps.narration: Operations in different orders give different rules.

steps.title: Expand A only
steps.action: Two multiplies x and four, producing two x plus eight.
steps.narration: B stays two x plus four.

steps.title: Compare at five
steps.action: A: five plus four, doubled, is eighteen; B: ten plus four is fourteen.
steps.narration: The outputs differ by four for this input.

worked_examples.repair: Keep two labelled machines side by side.

worked_examples.q: A fundraiser sells b booklets at R6 each, plus one R15 donation. Give F(b), fill totals for b=0,2,5, and check the claim F(b)=6(b+15).
worked_examples.answer: F(b)=6b+15; table totals R15, R27, R45; claim invalid.
states: R6 per booklet plus one R15 gift
Claim invalid; fixed gift is R15 once

steps.title: Separate variable and fixed parts
steps.action: Six times the booklet count changes; the fifteen-rand donation stays once.
steps.narration: The donation is not in every booklet.

steps.title: Fill the three input rows
steps.action: Zero booklets still leaves fifteen rand; two yield twenty seven, five yield forty five.
steps.narration: Use the same rule each time.

steps.title: Inspect the proposed bracket
steps.action: Six times fifteen would count ninety rand of donation.
steps.narration: This is the first mismatch with the context.

steps.title: State the corrected conclusion
steps.action: Six b plus fifteen fits all three rows and the original story.
steps.narration: A contextual reason and table both reject the claim.

worked_examples.verify: At b=0 true total R15 while claim gives R90; at b=5 true total R45.
worked_examples.misconception: Multiplying the one donation by every booklet.
worked_examples.repair: Place the gift as one separate tile before forming the rule.

5n rand
Cost is five repeated n times.
A flow doubles x then subtracts 3. Give rule and y at x=5.
x→2x→2x−3; at five, ten minus three equals seven.
Table inputs 1,2,3 give outputs 7,11,15. Give rule and output at 4.
Difference four; at x=1 offset three; outputs 7,11,15,19.
A rectangle has length x+4 cm and width 2 cm. Give simplified area and perimeter at x=3.
A=2x+8 cm²; P=2x+12 cm; at x=3, A=14 cm² and P=18 cm
A=2(x+4)=2x+8; P=2[(x+4)+2]=2x+12; at x=3, length 7, area 14 and perimeter 18.
Plan A charges R18 once plus R3 per visit. Plan B charges R6 per visit. Write both rules and compare at 4 visits. Explain why one input does not show the cheaper plan for every visit count.
A(v)=18+3v; B(v)=6v; at 4, A=R30, B=R24, B is R6 cheaper; one input is not a universal comparison.
At 4: A=18+12=30, B=24; at 10: A=48, B=60, so the relative price changes.
